sections.heading: In This Video
paragraphs: Omalizumab

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody and it is recombinant, it is similar to human immunoglobulin G1 and it targets human immunoglobulin E (IgE)

IgE immunoglobulin plays a critical role in activating mast cells during asthma attack (and allergic conditions in general) to release inflammatory mediators responsible for producing asthma symptoms, IgE also activates eosinophils and basophils

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: So by inhibiting IgE, Omalizumab works to inhibit mast cell degranulation and inhibit eosinophils and basophils => this lead to breaking the allergic cascade and control asthma symptoms

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: Omalizumab is administered subcutaneously and its absorption to systemic circulation is slow, peak plasma concentrations achieved after around 7 days
Omalizumab metabolized by the reticuloendothelial system and endothelial cells and eliminated through bile in around 25 days

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: Omalizumab is FDA approved for:
bullets: Treatment of moderate to severe asthma in patients (older than 6) whose symptoms not adequately controlled with inhaled corticosteroids; Omalizumab is not approved for use in acute asthmatic attacks
In treatment of chronic idiopathic or spontaneous urticaria, in patients (older than 12) who received H1 antihistamine treatment and still experiencing symptoms
It is also approved for patients (older than 18) for treatment of nasal polyps (in case the nasal corticosteroids didn’t work)

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: Off label uses:

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Omalizumab is a targeted therapy, that is why it is considered to have an excellent safety profile
Omalizumab may lead to the following
bullets: Anaphylactic reactions (in the second dose and after in 0.001 of cases)

sections.heading: Contraindications
paragraphs: Previous hypersensitivity reactions to omalizumab
Patients must be closely observed for several hours after omalizumab administration due to risk for anaphylaxis

sections.heading: In This Video
paragraphs: Mepolizumab & Reslizumab

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Mepolizumab and Reslizumab are humanized monoclonal antibodies and they are recombinant

They both work by binding to IL-5 and preventing it from binding to its receptor on the surface of the eosinophils => leading to inhibition of the signal for eosinophils proliferation, activation and survival in the bone marrow

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: Mepolizumab is available as SC only while reslizumab is available as IV only
Mepolizumab SC absorption is slow, it reaches peak plasma conc in 4-8 days after administration
Mepolizumab is metabolized by the proteolytic enzymes with a half life of 20 days

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: Reslizumab peak plasma conc are reached after the infusion (since it given IV)
Reslizumab is metabolized by proteolytic enzymes with a half life of 24 days

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: Mepolizumab is FDA approved for treatment of severe asthma and high eosinophils levels at 150 cell/mcL or higher (before treatment) in patients aged 12 and older, Mepolizumab also FDA approved for treatment of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and hypereosinophilic syndrome

Reslizumab is FDA approved for treatment of severe asthma and high eosinophils levels at 400 cell/mcL or higher (before treatment) with at least one asthma exacerbation in the previous year in patients aged 18 and older

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Both of these medications are targeted therapy, that is why it is considered to have an excellent safety profile
Mepolizumab may lead to:
bullets: Headache, back pain, abdominal pain and muscle spasms

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Reslizumab may lead to:

sections.heading: Contraindications
paragraphs: Previous hypersensitivity reactions to Mepolizumab and reslizumab
Patients must be closely observed for several hours after Mepolizumab/ reslizumab administration due to risk for anaphylaxis

sections.heading: In This Video
paragraphs: Mast cell stabilizers

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Cromolyn sodium is a mast cell stabilizer that inhibit mast cell degranulation => prevents release of inflammatory mediators including histamine and leukotrienes which cause allergic symptoms and bronchoconstriction

Ketotifen is an antihistamine and a mast cell stabilizer, it works by blocking histamine H1 receptors => less allergic symptoms; it also work as to prevent mast cell degranulation and inhibits release of inflammatory mediators (e.g. leukotrienes and histamine)

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: Cromolyn sodium is available as oral solution, nasal spray, ophthalmic solution, and inhalation solution
Cromolyn Oral absorption is really poor, bioavailability is around 0.5-2% and the majority of the medication (98%) excreted unchanged in the feces
Ketotifen is available is oral tablets/solution and ophthalmic solution

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: Cromolyn sodium is FDA approved for these therapeutic uses:
bullets: Prophylaxis of bronchial asthma attacks given as metered dose inhaler and nebulizer
Adjuvant treatment of allergic rhinitis given as intranasal
Systemic mast cell disease (mastocytosis) in pediatric and adult patients (oral solution)
Oral Cromolyn sodium solution is used to improve symptoms of diarrhea, flushing, headaches, vomiting, urticaria, abdominal pain and itching
Ophthalmic solution for treatment of allergic eye conditions (e.g. keratitis)
Cromolyn off label uses include prevention of serious reactions to foods and in management of IBS

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: Ketotifen in its oral form is FDA approved to prevent asthma attacks or anaphylaxis as well as preventing other allergic disorders
Ketotifen in its ophthalmic form is used to treat allergic conjunctivitis

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Cromolyn sodium is irritant material that caused local side effects depending on the site of administration:
bullets: Inhalational route: hoarseness, epiglottitis, laryngeal and pharyngeal edema, bronchial irritation, cough and pulmonary infiltrates
Intranasal route: nasal congestion, sneezing, nasal itching, nosebleeds and headaches
Ophthalmic solution: eye dryness, itchiness and puffiness
Cromolyn oral solution may lead to: headache, diarrhea, pruritus, nausea, myalgia, abdominal pain, vomiting, urticaria, angioedema

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Ketotifen oral route side effects: drowsiness, weight gain, dry mouth, irritability, nosebleeds, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headaches and fatigue; it may also lead to anaphylaxis, liver dysfunction, blood disorders and seizure disorders
Ketotifen eye drops may lead to eye redness, eye swelling, eye itching, pain and eye discomfort

sections.heading: Contraindications
paragraphs: Both medications are contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity reactions to them

sections.heading: Overdose
paragraphs: Ketotifen overdose: sedation, confusion, disorientation, agitation, hallucinations, ataxia, tremor, myoclonus, nystagmus, dysarthria and slurred speech, tachycardia, hypotension, cardiac arrest, pulmonary edema, pancreatitis, hepatitis
Overdose is rare with Cromolyn sodium because of the low bioavailability

sections.heading: Video Contents
paragraphs: Muscarinic receptor antagonists

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Muscarinic receptor antagonists (inhaled ipratropium) work by competitively blocking the muscarinic M3 receptors in the airways smooth muscles leading to indirect bronchodilatation through unopposed B2 adrenergic action
Ipratropium also work to decrease bronchial secretions

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Ipratropium also blocks M2 receptors (M2 receptors function as feedback regulators, inhibiting acetylcholine release) so once inhibited, there is increase in acetylcholine release and reduction in extent and duration of ipratropium blockage on M3 receptors; this may lead to paradoxical bronchoconstriction
Ipratropium is not sufficient alone for asthma treatment. It is usually combined with Beta 2 agonist to get synergistic effect

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: Available formulations: nasal spray, metered dose inhaler, and nebulized solution
Duration of action is around 4 hours

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: Asthma: according to GINA guidelines, ipratropium is used in acute severe asthma, particularly if the patient is having altered mental status or silent chest; and ipratropium is given with SABA, oxygen and system steroids
COPD: according to GOLD guidelines, SABA with/without ipratropium is the initial bronchodilator for acute treatment of COPD exacerbation along with supportive measures

sections.heading: Video Contents
paragraphs: Methylxanthines

sections.heading: Methylxanthines examples
paragraphs: Caffeine, theophylline, theobromine and aminophylline (salt of theophylline)
Methylxanthines that are used in treatment of asthma include theophylline and aminophylline

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Methylxanthines work by non competitively inhibiting phosphodiesterase enzyme (PDE III and PDE IV) => increase cAMP, cGMP levels leading to:
bullets: Relaxation of all smooth muscles (bronchial smooth muscles, GIT, biliary, ureteric...)
Cardiac stimulation: increase cardiac contractility and arrhythmogenic effects
Vasoconstriction of cerebral blood vessels and vasodilatation of peripheral blood vessels

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Methylxanthines also work by antagonizing adenosine receptors A1, A2 and A3, leading to:
bullets: Adenosine is bronchoconstrictor so blocking its receptors => bronchodilatation
Adenosine has inhibitory effect on CNS (it signals mental fatigue) so blocking its receptors => CNS stimulation

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Methylxanthines also work as Histone deacetylase activator, Histone deacetylase work to prevent inflammation, so activating it lead to anti inflammatory effect and that work in the benefit of asthma

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: Oral methylxanthines have broadly fluctuating plasma drug concentrations which made it fall out of favor in clinical use
IV formulas have more consistent plasma drug concentrations and it is used more

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: Respiratory uses: FDA approved theophylline and aminophylline in treatment of asthma, bronchitis and emphysema, new GINA guidelines (2018) don’t recommend it anymore in treatment of asthma, same as GOLD guidelines don’t recommend it in COPD treatment
bullets: Chronic bronchial asthma: oral theophylline is used (as a second line) in treatment of chronic asthma
Acute severe asthma: IV aminophylline are indicated for termination of acute bronchospasm in asthma attack

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: CNS uses:
bullets: To delay physical and mental fatigue (caffeine)
Treatment of migraine (caffeine + ergotamine): to increase vasoconstriction of cerebral blood vessels and increase absorption of ergotamine from GIT
Neonatal apnea syndrome: caffeine is the agent of choice
CVS uses: acute pulmonary edema due to left side HF

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Methylxanthines have a narrow therapeutic index, this means there is a high incidence of side effects
bullets: CNS: irritability, headache, insomnia, nervousness and convulsions
CVS: palpitations, tachycardia, and arrhythmias. Rapid IV injection can cause hypotension, syncope and cardiac arrest
GIT: nausea, anorexia, hyperacidity and worsening of peptic ulcer

sections.heading: Precautions
paragraphs: Aminophylline must be given by slow IV infusion (> 15 minutes to avoid syncope and cardiac arrest)
Used with caution in CVS disease, hepatic impairment, hypo or hyperthyroidism, seizure disorder or pregnancy
They should not be given to patients with peptic ulcer because it lead to hyperacidity

sections.heading: Drug interactions
paragraphs: Methylxanthines are metabolized by the liver CYP enzyme system, and since they have narrow therapeutic index, this means that they are highly affected by CYP enzyme inhibitors (e.g. erythromycin) leading to higher serum levels of methylxanthines and toxicity; and also they are highly affected by CYP enzyme inducers (e.g. smoking) leading to decrease their serum levels and reduce effect
There is increased risk of arrhythmia when combining Beta 2 agonists and methylxanthines in the same time because both have arrhythmogenic

sections.heading: Video contents
paragraphs: Corticosteroids

sections.heading: Why NSAIDs can’t be given in bronchial asthma
paragraphs: Because NSAIDs inhibit COX enzyme but not lipoxygenase enzyme leading to accumulation of leukotrienes which are potent bronchoconstrictors
Aspirin induced asthma

sections.heading: Corticosteroids
paragraphs: Corticosteroids work by inhibiting phospholipase A2 enzyme leading to less arachidonic acid and less synthesis of prostaglandins and leukotrienes which ultimately lead to anti inflammatory effect

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Corticosteroids can effectively decrease bronchial inflammation and hyperresponsiveness through:
bullets: They inhibit B cell function => decrease antibody release and subsequently decrease antigen-antibody reaction
They inhibit T cell function => decrease mediators and cytokine release
They inhibit macrophage activity and stabilize lysosomal membranes => less inflammation
They inhibit mast cells => decrease histamine release and lowers capillary permeability
Corticosteroids cause up regulation of B2 receptors because it lowers inflammation => better response to b2 agonists medications

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Their onset of action is gradual and may take anywhere from several days to several weeks for maximal benefit with consistent use

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: There is oral, IV and inhaled formulations
Inhaled formulations include liquid capsule formulation given through nebulizer, metered dose inhalers and dry powder inhalers
Widely used ICS include budesonide, fluticasone and beclomethasone

sections.heading: Use in asthma
paragraphs: In acute severe asthmatic attack: IV hydrocortisone
Chronic asthma
bullets: ICS: Inhaled corticosteroids (e.g. beclomethasone): FDA indicated treatment of choice for preventing asthma exacerbations in patient with persistent asthma; regular use of these medications reduce frequency of asthma symptoms, bronchial hyperresponsiveness and risk of serious exacerbations; they have minimal systemic side effects, but an appropriate inhalation technique is critical for success of therapy

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are associated with much less systemic side effects compared to oral and IV corticosteroids, but it may lead to some local side effects:
bullets: Dysphonia in 50% of the patients due to myopathy of laryngeal muscles an mucosal irritation
Oropharyngeal candidiasis due to corticosteroid decreasing mouth immunity; this can be avoided by rinsing the mouth after each inhalation and can be treated by nystatin mouthwash or miconazole
Reduction in growth velocity in children using them, these effects in low doses are small and reversible but in higher doses they are significant
ICS may rarely lead to cataract, glaucoma, hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis dysfunction and impaired glucose metabolism

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Oral and IV corticosteroids lead to systemic adverse effects, including:
bullets: Cushingoid features (truncal obesity, buffalo hump and moon face)
Ecchymosis, skin thinning, stria and impaired wound healing

sections.heading: Precautions
paragraphs: Oral or IV corticosteroids if used for a long period of time, must be withdrawn gradually to avoid acute Addisonian crisis
Corticosteroid lowers potassium levels so Diet should be rich in K
Continuous check for any increase in weight, edema, sugar in urine or BP
If the patient develops acute infection, they must be treated by adequate antibiotics with decreased dose of steroids

sections.heading: In This Video
paragraphs: Anti Leukotrienes include Leukotriene receptor antagonists and Leukotriene synthesis inhibitors

sections.heading: Agents
paragraphs: Leukotriene receptors antagonists

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Inside many inflammatory cells, Leukotrienes are synthesized from Arachidonic acid by the action of the Lipoxygenase enzyme
Leukotrienes are powerful bronchoconstrictors, they also lead to increase vascular permeability (edema), mucus secretion and inflammation; and they are highly expressed in asthma

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Montelukast and Zafirlukast work by antagonizing the leukotrienes Cys-LT1 receptors => less bronchoconstriction
Zileuton works by inhibiting the 5-lipoxygenase enzyme => less leukotrienes => less bronchoconstriction

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: All of these medications are available as oral formula only
Montelukast and Zileuton has very good absorption even with food while Zafirlukast has to be taken on an empty stomach
Those are taken as once or twice daily doses

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: Montelukast is used in prophylaxis and treatment of chronic asthma in patients of all ages while Zafirlukast indicated in prophylaxis and treatment of chronic asthma in children aged 5 and older and adults; and Zileuton is used in prophylaxis and treatment of chronic asthma in patients aged 12 and older
Montelukast is preferred over corticosteroids in prophylaxis and treatment of asthma in children because:
bullets: Corticosteroids may cause growth retardation in children
In clinical trials, leukotriene receptor antagonists reduced frequency of asthma exacerbations as equal as corticosteroids did

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: Montelukast is used in prevention of exercise induced bronchospasm
Montelukast is used in the relief of symptoms of allergic rhinitis as a second line (the first line for moderate/severe allergic rhinitis is intranasal glucocorticoids)
Zafirlukast off label uses include allergic rhinitis and prophylaxis against exercise induced bronchospasm

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: Zileuton is used off label in treatment of aspirin induced asthma, COPD, acne, pruritus in Sjogren Larsson syndrome and atopic dermatitis
All of these medications have no role in treatment of acute severe asthma

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: All of these medications are well tolerated, but Zafirlukast is better tolerated than Montelukast and Zileuton; all may lead to headaches, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fatigue and upper respiratory tract infection

Montelukast and Zileuton may lead to neuropsychiatric disorder (including depression, aggression, suicidal ideation, insomnia, anxiety and nightmares), allergic granulomatous angiitis and immune system disorders

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Zafirlukast and Zileuton may lead to elevation of liver enzymes, acute hepatitis and hyperbilirubinemia
In case of Zileuton, LFTs has to be ordered before starting treatment and it should be monitored
Symptoms of hepatotoxicity include abdominal pain, edema, pruritus, and yellowish discoloration of the skin and mucus membranes

sections.heading: Contraindications
paragraphs: All of these medications are contraindicated in case of hypersensitivity reactions
Zafirlukast and Zileuton are contraindicated in hepatic impairment

sections.heading: Drug interactions
paragraphs: Zileuton is microsomal enzyme inhibitor and can inhibit the metabolism of many drugs e.g. warfarin and theophylline

sections.heading: Video contents
paragraphs: Beta 2 adrenergic agonists

sections.heading: Beta adrenergic agonists classification
paragraphs: Non selective Beta adrenergic agonists: e.g. adrenaline and ephedrine
Selective Beta 2 agonists:
bullets: SABA (short acting beta agonist): salbutamol, terbutaline (duration of action is around 3-6 hours)
LABA (long acting beta agonist): salmeterol and formoterol (duration of action is around 10 hours)
Ultra LABA: indacaterol (duration of action is around 24 hours)

sections.heading: Administration
paragraphs: Routes of administration for these medications: metered dosed inhalers, nebulizers, dry powder inhalers, orally, subcutaneously or intravenously; inhalation being the preferred route (less side effects)
In acute asthma: they are given by inhalation or IV infusion
In chronic asthma: they are given orally or by inhalation

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: They work on the respiratory system by Multiple mechanisms:
bullets: Activation of bronchial Beta 2 receptors, will lead to increase cAMP levels which lead to airway smooth muscle relaxation and bronchodilatation

Beta 2 agonists are thought to also work as anti-inflammatory on the airways by reducing intracellular adhesion molecule 1, reducing granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factors release and stabilizing the mast cells (less histamine release)

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Tachycardia and arrhythmia due to
bullets: Direct activation of cardiac beta 1 receptors (it is selective but not that selective)
In skeletal muscle blood vessels, same beta 2 receptors are present, when activated it would lead to vasodilatation => hypotension => reflex tachycardia
Tremors caused by skeletal muscle beta 2 receptors activation

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Tolerance with prolonged use (require temporary cessation of the drug)
Hypokalemia (due to shift of potassium from blood to cells) => they are used in treatment of hyperkalemia
Excessive sweating, anxiety, insomnia and agitation due to activation of sympathetic nervous system

sections.heading: Antiepileptic drugs classification
paragraphs: First generation (Classic) drugs: Phenytoin; Carbamazepine; Valproic acid; Ethosuximide; Phenobarbital; Benzodiazepines
Second generation (newer) drugs: Vigabatrin; Lamotrigine; Topiramate; Levetiracetam; Gabapentin & pregabalin; Tiagabine

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Trade name: Zarontin
The least toxic antiepileptic drug
It is mainly used in treatment of absence seizures
Ethosuximide was first synthesized in 1957 and was a big help to children with absence seizures

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Ethosuximide work by blocking the T type Ca+2 channels in thalamocortical neurons

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: First line drug for treatment of absence seizures
It can be used as monotherapy for absence seizures, unless generalized tonic clonic seizures are associated with the absence seizures and in that case valproate is preferred

sections.heading: Dosing
paragraphs: In children
bullets: In adults: Starting dose is 250 mg/day and titrated up until response occur

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Ethosuximide is well tolerated and less toxic than other antiepileptic
bullets: GIT symptoms: abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting
It may rarely lead to psychosis, depression and lupus

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: Ethosuximide is available as oral formulations in form of capsules and oral suspension
Absorption is almost complete with bioavailability of 90% and peak plasma levels reached within 3 hours after oral administration
Distribution: ethosuximide doesn’t bind to plasma proteins and readily crosses the BBB to exert its effects

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: 80% of Ethosuximide dose is metabolized by the liver mainly by CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites
20% is excreted unchanged in the urine
Its half life is around 40 hours

sections.heading: Drug interactions
paragraphs: Valproic acid inhibit ethosuximide metabolism and decrease ethosuximide clearance leading to higher concentrations of the drug in the blood

sections.heading: Contraindications
paragraphs: Hypersensitivity reactions to the medications itself or to the succinimides family of medications

sections.heading: Antiepileptic drugs classification

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Famous trade name: Neurontin
Gabapentin is an analog of GABA, but it doesn’t work on the GABA receptors
It was discovered in 1975 by Satzinger & Hartenstein and got FDA approval for treatment of epilepsy in 1993

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: It doesn’t work at the GABA receptors

The precise mechanism is not fully understood, but it seem to be related to inhibiting the alpha 2 delta voltage gated calcium channels => that lead to decrease the excitatory neurotransmitters release into the synapse

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: It is FDA approved for treatment of:
bullets: Add on therapy for focal onset seizures
Moderate to severe restless leg syndrome
Off label uses: Other types of neuropathic pain: e.g. diabetic neuropathy and trigeminal neuralgia, it is NOT used for sciatica
Fibromyalgia, bipolar disorder, anxiety, mood disorders, depression, IBS, alcohol withdrawal, headache ...

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: CNS: ataxia

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: CNS: nystagmus

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Headache, tremor and dizziness
Fatigue and sleepiness
Most of these adverse effects occur initially in the start of the treatment and go away with time

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Rarely may lead to suicidal ideation, Steven Johnson syndrome, respiratory depression and rhabdomyolysis

Withdrawal symptoms occur after abrupt stopping of this medications, patient agitated, confused and disoriented followed by GI complaint and sweating, tremor tachycardia, hypertension and insomnia also occur
Dependence also occur with this medication

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: Gabapentin is absorbed via LAT2 amino acid transporter in the upper intestine, this absorption system is saturable, this lead to bioavailability of 80% if only 100 mg is given per dose and 60% bioavailability if 300mg given and so on
Gabapentin is not bound to plasma proteins, the full dose get distributed to body tissues including the brain

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: Gabapentin undergoes minimal metabolism
Eliminated renally with short Elimination half life of around 6 hours

sections.heading: Dosing
paragraphs: Initially start with 300 mg/ day and titrate up to 3 times per day of the same dose, max dose is 4800 mg/day
In renal impairment dose should be reduced

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Famous trade name: Keppra
Broad spectrum antiepileptic and one of the most commonly prescribed antiepileptics because it has less adverse effects
Levetiracetam was first approved for medical use in 1999 in US for treatment of epilepsy

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Levetiracetam binds to SV2A protein and inhibits it
SV2A is a synaptic vesicle membrane proteins, SV2A function is to help in the process of exocytosis of the excitatory neurotransmitters into the synapse
Inhibiting SV2A by the levetiracetam lead to less excitatory neurotransmitters released to the synapse

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: Broad spectrum antiepileptic activity
Can be used as monotherapy or as an add on
It’s FDA approved for: Focal seizures in adults and children; Idiopathic generalized onset tonic clonic seizures; Myoclonic seizures of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy in adolescents older than 12

sections.heading: Off-label uses
paragraphs: It is used off label for: Status epilepticus; For prophylaxis against seizures in subarachnoid hemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, palliative care

sections.heading: Adverse effects — ataxia
paragraphs: CNS: ataxia

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Dizziness
Lack of energy
It also lead to leukopenia, eosinophilia and rarely pancytopenia

sections.heading: Behavioral and hypersensitivity effects
paragraphs: Less commonly may lead to behavioral and mood changes such as irritability, aggression, agitation, anger, psychosis, anxiety, depression and emotional liability
Rarely lead to hypersensitivity reactions in form of spreading rash progressing to SJS and TEN

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: Available as oral and intravenous formulations
Rapidly absorbed from the GI tract with 95% bioavailability, food slows absorption but doesn’t affect amount absorbed
Distribution: the drug is protein bound by 10%, the rest is distributed to body tissues

sections.heading: Metabolism and elimination
paragraphs: 30% of the drug is metabolized by enzymatic hydrolysis of acetamide group in the blood (the liver has minimal role) and the rest excreted unchanged in urine
Plasma half life is around 7 hours

sections.heading: Dosing
paragraphs: IV is the same as oral dose
There is no loading dose
Adult dosing: start with 500 mg twice daily and titrate up until response occur, titration every two weeks by 250-500 mg and max dose is 3000 mg

sections.heading: Pediatric dosing
paragraphs: Pediatrics: used in children older than 5 years, start with 20 mg/kg per divided into 2 doses and titrate up by 20 mg/kg every 2 weeks, max dose is 60 mg/kg

sections.heading: Drug interactions
paragraphs: Minimal drug interactions

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Trade name: Lamictal
It is one of the most widely prescribed antiepileptics in treatment of focal seizures
It was first used in 1990 in Ireland to treat epilepsy

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: It blocks voltage gated sodium channels (similar to most of the first Gen antiepileptics)
It also inhibit the presynaptic release of glutamate and aspartate

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: It is effective in treatment of focal seizures (same with the carbamazepine)
It is also effective against idiopathic generalized onset tonic clonic seizures and Lennox Gastaut syndrome

sections.heading: Other therapeutic uses
paragraphs: It is also effective in treatment of Absence seizures (but not as effective as ethosuximide or valproate)
Preferred in pregnancy due to low teratogenic potential
It used off label in treatment of bipolar disorder, fibromyalgia, schizophrenia and depression

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Lamotrigine is generally well tolerated but it may lead to:
Headache
Nausea and vomiting

sections.heading: Adverse effects — diplopia
paragraphs: CNS: diplopia

sections.heading: Rash and insomnia
paragraphs: Skin rash (allergic) and rarely progresses to SJS (higher risk if combined with valproic acid)
Insomnia (most antiepileptics cause sedation instead)

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: Lamotrigine is well absorbed with bioavailability of 98%
Distribution: binds to proteins by 55%, the rest is distributed to the tissues especially the brain where it exert its effects, Vd is 1.2

sections.heading: Metabolism and elimination
paragraphs: It is metabolized by glucuronidation in the liver and excreted in urine
Eliminated by first order kinetics and Half life is around 24 hours

sections.heading: Drug interactions
paragraphs: Lamotrigine is commonly combined with valproate, valproate inhibits lamotrigine metabolism leading to increase of its drug levels and half life
So lamotrigine dose should be reduced if combined with valproate

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Buprenorphine is synthetic opioid, it works as a mixed agonist/antagonist (partial agonist)
It was synthesized in late 1960s, it is a derivative of thebaine
It is famous for its use in treatment of pain and opioid misuse disorder

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: Available in sublingual, buccal, transdermal, IV, IM formulas
Bioavailability of sublingual is 30%, and buccal is 65%
Metabolized by the liver by CYP3A4 and CYP2C8

sections.heading: Onset and elimination
paragraphs: Onset of action is after 30 minutes of administration, elimination half life is around 37 hours and duration of action is about 20 hours
Excreted through kidney and liver

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Buprenorphine act as a potent partial agonist at mu opioid receptor and antagonist on kappa and delta receptors (mixed agonist antagonist), compared to morphine for equivalent dose, buprenorphine sublingual is around 50 times more potent than morphine and 100 times more potent if used as a transdermal patch
Buprenorphine can displace full mu agonists (e.g. morphine) because it is more potent, leading to withdrawal symptoms in opioid physically dependent patients

sections.heading: Pharmacologic effect
paragraphs: Buprenorphine provides analgesia that is good for moderate to severe pain, but it can antagonize the analgesic effects of agonist opioids (e.g. morphine) if it used when they are being used on a patient because it produces less effect when it bind to the opioid receptors compared to the full agonist opioids
Buprenorphine provides less euphoric effects thus it provides less abuse potential than agonist opioids

sections.heading: Receptor dissociation
paragraphs: The risk of respiratory depression is lower when compared to agonist opioids
It slowly dissociates from the receptors its occupying so that is why it has long duration of action and mild withdrawal symptoms once withdrawn

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: Used in treatment of chronic pain (as transdermal patch), it has a long duration (24 hours)

Also used in treatment of opioid addiction (same with methadone) because of its long duration of action, providing less withdrawal symptoms when withdrawn and blocking the effects of any agonist opioid if they are used during the buprenorphine effect period

sections.heading: Combination with naloxone
paragraphs: It is proven that it has shorter and less severe withdrawal symptoms compared to methadone

Buprenorphine when used in treatment of opioid misuse disorder, it is used in combination with naloxone and used sublingual or buccal, because this combination if used intravenously, the naloxone would be absorbed and it would bind into opioid receptors leading to acute withdrawal (so it can’t be used intravenously, thus the patient can’t abuse it)

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Buprenorphine doesn’t cause respiratory depression unless it is very high dose but once it causes Respiratory depression, it can’t be reversed by naloxone
The risk of respiratory depression is higher if buprenorphine is injected IV with benzodiazepines
Increased blood pressure because it increase systemic and pulmonary vascular resistance leading

sections.heading: Other adverse effects
paragraphs: Prolongation of QT interval (risky in cardiovascular diseases)
Psychotomimetic effects such as hallucinations, nightmare and anxiety have been reported after use of drugs with mixed agonist antagonistic actions
Mu make the most euphoria and since they don’t activate mu that much so addiction is low

sections.heading: Gastrointestinal and neurologic effects
paragraphs: Nausea and vomiting
Constipation
Headache, mild amnesia, cognitive and neural inhibition
Pruritus
Risk of seizures if used in epilepsy patients

sections.heading: Pupillary and urinary effects
paragraphs: Miosis
Urinary retention

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Tramadol is a synthetic opioid analgesic medication
Synthesized in 1963 in Germany and used commercially in 1977 under trade name Tramal
It is famous for producing less euphoria compared to other opioids, thus it is less addictive

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
paragraphs: Available as oral formulas, also available as IV, IM and rectal formulas
Well absorbed with 70% oral bioavailability and 77% rectal

It undergoes extensive metabolism via CYP2D6 in the liver leading to desmethyltramadol which has more affinity to mu receptors and thus it is more active and lead to most of tramadol analgesic effects, some people has different variations of this enzyme that convert tramadol into inactive metabolites with no analgesic action

sections.heading: Elimination
paragraphs: Excreted through the kidney
Tramadol Elimination half life is about 9 hours

sections.heading: Mechanism of action
paragraphs: Tramadol Bind to opioid receptors, especially mu receptors but it has low affinity to these receptors, it undergoes extensive metabolism via CYP2D6 leading to active metabolite which has much higher affinity for mu receptors which lead to its analgesic effects
It also block the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, so it increase their levels and may lead to serotonin syndrome (this is opposite to morphine, because morphine decreases norepinephrine)

sections.heading: Central pharmacologic effects
paragraphs: Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several central effects (CNS effects):
Analgesia: tramadol has one tenth the analgesic potency of morphine, means that tramadol has equal potency with pethidine and codeine, tramadol analgesia last for 6 hours
Euphoria: less euphoria than other opioids
Sedation
Respiratory depression: less than morphine
Cough suppression
Nausea and vomiting
Miosis
Pruritus due to histamine release

sections.heading: Peripheral pharmacologic effects
paragraphs: Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several peripheral effects including:
CVS: bradycardia and hypotension
GIT: constipation
Urinary system: may lead to urine retention
Immune: decrease immunity

sections.heading: Therapeutic uses
paragraphs: Used in treatment of moderate to severe pain – analgesic effect start after 1 hour of ingestion and it lasts for 6 hours
Used as a second line in treatment of fibromyalgia (first line being either pregabalin or duloxetine)
Also used in treatment of refractory restless legs syndrome (other opioids also effective in treatment of this condition)

sections.heading: Adverse effects
paragraphs: Nausea and vomiting
Dry mouth
Headache, drowsiness
Respiratory depression

sections.heading: Dependence and neuropsychiatric effects
paragraphs: Tolerance, physical dependence
Numbness, tingling, paresthesia, tinnitus due to increased serotonin and norepinephrine
Psychiatric symptoms: hallucinations, paranoia, anxiety, confusion due to increased serotonin

sections.heading: Seizures and toxicity
paragraphs: It may induce seizures in epileptic patients (relative contraindication)
Administration of naloxone can only partially reverse tramadol toxicity

sections.heading: Interactions
paragraphs: Tramadol interact with other medications that increase serotonin levels (e.g. SSRIs) and may lead to serotonin syndrome

sections.heading: Contraindications
paragraphs: Pregnancy and lactation: due to neonatal withdrawal syndrome
Children under 12 and elderly due to high risk of respiratory depression
Liver and kidney failure due to accumulation

sections.heading: Surgical needles
paragraphs: Used to carry the suture material into the tissue
Should be: Strong, Sharp, Slim, Sterile
Needle components: End, Body, Tip

sections.heading: Needle end
paragraphs: It is the portion where the suture material is attached to
It is either swaged (eyeless) needles (suture materials connect to the inside of the needle) and there is the eyed needles where suture material connected to the eye of the needle
In swaged needles only one strand of the suture material is attached to the needle and it meant for single use only

In eyed needles two strands of the material is carried one going into the needles and the other outgoing from the needle and the needle size is bigger compared to eyeless needles and this produce bigger holes in the tissue means more tissue trauma and more infection possibility but those are cost effective

sections.heading: Needle body
paragraphs: Needle body is either curved or straight and there is degrees to each

sections.heading: Needle tip
paragraphs: It is the part that penetrate the tissue, and it is classified according to its cross section
Round bodied - tapered: Muscle, fascia, peritoneum, viscera
Round bodied - Blunt: friable tissue
Cutting: Dense tissue like skin and tendons
Reverse cutting: Skin

GCS 9–12 = moderate injury

Interobserver reliability is imperfect

sections.heading: Suturing materials
paragraphs: Used to hold tissue together while in healing phase
Suturing material should be: Sterile; Cause minimal tissue reaction; Strong
If the suturing happen in tissues where absorption of the suture material is necessary then the material should be capable to be absorbed by the tissues once healing phase complete

sections.heading: Types of suturing materials
paragraphs: Absorbable: Natural, Synthetic
Non absorbable: Natural, Synthetic

sections.heading: Absorbable materials
paragraphs: Materials that absorbed by the body by enzymes or hydrolysis
Absorption cause these materials to weaken progressively until they get absorbed fully
Rate of absorption is the speed by which the body absorb these materials and it is determined by the type of material used and the body part being sutured and the patient factors
In optimal situation, absorption process start when the wound get adequate strength
Absorbable materials used for suturing deeper layers of the body because suture removal is not possible, and also used for areas that heal rapidly

sections.heading: Types and uses of absorbable materials
paragraphs: Catgut (natural): Not commonly used
Chromic catgut (natural): Closure of mucosal wounds; Not commonly used
Polyglactin aka Vicryl (synthetic): Suturing of deep tissues, percutaneous closure; Most frequently used, retains strength for 3 weeks
Monocryl (synthetic): Useful as buried suture, retains strength for less than month
Polydioxanone aka PDS (synthetic): Useful for wounds that require prolonged dermal support, support longer than Vicryl

sections.heading: Non absorbable materials
paragraphs: Those materials are not absorbed by the body and they stay in the tissues and they get walled off by the inflammatory process or they are removed manually
They preferred when long term tissue support is needed such as in tissues that heal slowly (vascular ligation, anastomoses) and also used for muscles, tendons, fascia and superficial wounds

sections.heading: Classification and uses of non absorbable materials
paragraphs: Class I: Silk (natural) => used for securing drains
Class I: Nylon (synthetic) => skin suturing, buried sutures that require prolonged dermal support
Class I: Polypropylene aka prolene (synthetic) => skin sutures, areas with anticipated swelling
Class II: Cotton (natural) => not commonly used
Class II: Linen (natural) => used generally when tissue support for long time not required
Class III: Surgical steel (natural) => orthopedic procedures, skin closure, hernial repair

sections.heading: Another classification of sutures
paragraphs: Monofilament
Multifilament (braided)

sections.heading: Size of suture materials
paragraphs: Suture materials assigned a number for size in reverse order, this means the higher the number the smaller the size and those have different uses
0-0 and 1-0: Abdominal wall closure and securing drains
2-0 and 3-0: Closure of thick tissues (skin, facia, muscles, tendons)
4-0 and 5-0: Closure of skin (hands, face, feet, pediatric patients)
6-0 and 7-0: Plastic surgery and blood vessels repair
8-0 to 11-0: Ophthalmic surgery and microvascular reconstruction

paragraphs: Aspirin inhibits cyclooxygenase enzyme and this includes both COX-1 and COX-2.
It irreversibly inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes.
Reduces thromboxane and PG levels in the body.

sections.heading: Aspirin uses
paragraphs: Analgesic effect.
Antipyretic effect: Reduce prostaglandin synthesis in the CNS.
Anti-inflammatory.
Antiplatelet: through inhibiting COX-1 in the platelets

sections.heading: Dosage
paragraphs: Low dose (less than 325mg) works on platelet aggregation.
Medium dose (325-1250mg) works as antipyretic and analgesic.
High dose (1250-4000) works as anti-inflammatory.

sections.heading: Adverse effects

Reye’s syndrome.

sections.heading: Definition and etiology
paragraphs: Inflammation of pancreas caused by activation of pancreatic enzymes => autodigestion
Overstimulation of pancreas: in alcoholic patients, and high dietary fat
Duct obstruction: obstruction of pancreatic duct => interstitial edema, impaired blood flow and acinar injury => activation of enzymes and autodigestion
Gallstones; Sickle cell disease, Cystic fibrosis (inherited); Choledochal cysts, Pancreas divisum (congenital)
Direct acinar cells injury: releases of proenzymes and further injury and activation of enzymes => autodigestion
Alcohol, drugs (Azathioprine, hydrochlorothiazide, Pentamidine); Trauma; Ischemia; Hypertriglyceridemia, Hypercalcemia, hyperthyroidism; infections
Defective intracellular transport: intracellular activation of enzymes => acinar cell injury => autodigestion
Alcohol; Duct obstruction

sections.heading: Severe acute pancreatitis
paragraphs: In severe acute pancreatitis, there is release of cytokines, toxic enzymes, and mediators into the circulation and activation of systemic inflammatory response, and this leads to:
Leukocytosis; DIC; ARDS; Hemolysis; Peripheral vascular collapse; Shock
Medical emergency

sections.heading: Patient presentation — history
paragraphs: Severe epigastric pain with radiation to the back, aggravated by meals
Nausea
Vomiting
Anorexia
Low grade fever

sections.heading: Patient presentation — examination
paragraphs: Epigastric tenderness
Abdominal distension (epigastric region)
Palpable abdominal mass (if pseudocyst developed)
Decreased bowel sounds
Jaundice
Tachycardia => because of pain, dehydration
Hypotension => dehydration, sepsis because of infection
Cullen’s sign => discoloration of the periumbilical region
Grey Turner’s sign => discoloration of the flanks

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: Labs: Serum lipase more specific than amylase, and it is elevated within 4 to 8 hours, peaks in 24 hours and remain elevated for 1 to 2 weeks
LFT: if elevated => gallstone pancreatitis, RFT
Blood glucose, Ca level, CBC, lipid profile, serum LDH
CRP
Imaging: AXR/CXR: pleural effusion, ARDS
CT: useful for complications
ERCP: reserved for therapeutic interventions
MRCP: diagnostic use

sections.heading: Ranson’s criteria
paragraphs: Predict the prognosis of acute pancreatitis
At admission: Age > 55 years; WBC > 16000 cell/mm3; Glucose > 200 mg/dl; LDH > 350 IU/L; AST > 250 U/L
During 48 hours: Hematocrit fall > 10%; BUN rise > 5 mg/dl; PaO2 < 60 mmHg; Base deficit > 5 mEq/L; Serum calcium < 2 mmol/L; Fluid sequestration > 6 L

sections.heading: Interpretation
paragraphs: Ranson score of 3 or more indicate severe acute pancreatitis
Ranson score also predict mortality
Less than 3: Less than 1%
More than 6: 100%

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Bowel rest (NPO) and restart feeding after resolution but if there is severe inflammation then inducing early enteral feeding is important
IVF, ringer lactate is preferred unless hypercalcemia is the cause of acute pancreatitis, first 24h from 2500–4000ml total, and then accordingly
Analgesia: acetaminophen if mild pain, tramadol, meperidine
Antibiotics: cover enteric anaerobic and aerobic microorganisms, imipenem, ampicillin, ceftriaxone
ERCP for gallstone pancreatitis
Drainage of infected pancreatic collections
Surgical: necrosectomy

sections.heading: Complications
paragraphs: Local: Necrosis => inflammation; Pseudocysts, Pancreatic abscess => disruption of the pancreatic duct
Systemic: ARDS => microthrombi in the pulmonary vessels; Hypocalcemia => sequestration of calcium in fat necrosis; Hyperglycemia => disruption of islets of Langerhans; Shock and dehydration; DIC
GIT complications: GIT bleeding => gastric or duodenal erosions from pancreatic enzymes; Jaundice => compression by pseudocyst or gallstones pancreatitis

sections.heading: Definition and etiology
paragraphs: Inflammation of the appendix, acute abdomen, very common
Inflammation then obstruction: most of the cases. Infection with E coli (aerobic) and bacteroides fragilis (unaerobic) mostly
Inflammation without obstruction

Obstruction then inflammation: Pediatric: Luminal obstruction that occurs as a result of lymphoid hyperplasia. Adults: luminal obstruction due to fecaliths, fibrosis, foreign bodies (food, parasites, calculi) or neoplasia

Luminal obstruction leads to bacterial overgrowth and inflammation and continued mucus secretion and exudation which leads to increased intraluminal pressure and referred visceral pain in periumbilical region, resolution can occur in this point but if not increased intraluminal pressure leads to impaired venous drainage and mucosal ischemia leading to gangrene and peritonitis

sections.heading: Patient presentation — history
paragraphs: Anorexia first symptom in 95% of patients
Visceral-somatic pain sequence: poorly localized abdominal pain that shifts to right iliac fossa after 4–6 hours
Vomiting once or twice
Nausea
Low grade pyrexia (37.2–37.7) start after 6 hours of the onset of the abdominal pain
In adult female you want to make sure that you put on your DDx ovarian torsion/cyst, ectopic pregnancy, PID

sections.heading: Patient presentation — examination
paragraphs: Localized abdominal tenderness especially in the McBurney’s point (2/3 the distance between umbilicus and the ASIS)
Muscle guarding
Rebound tenderness
Pointing sign (patient pointing where pain began and where it moved to)
Rovsing’s sign (deep palpation in left iliac fossa cause pain in right iliac fossa)
Psoas sign (patient lie on their left side and examiner extend their right thigh => if patient feel pain then sign is positive and indicate inflamed retrocecal appendix)
Obturator sign (patient flex their right knee and examiner slowly internally rotate the right hip => if patient fell pain then sign is positive and indicate inflamed pelvic appendix)

sections.heading: Patient presentation — pregnancy and young children
paragraphs: Pregnant females: Diagnosis difficult and delayed because early features maybe attributed to pregnancy; upward displacement of the caecum will change the pain location to RUQ
Treatment is operative as perforation carries high maternal and fetal mortality

Children less than 3 years of age: Rare but carries higher morbidity and mortality because patient can’t give history => diagnosis to be delayed; diffuse peritonitis develop rapidly because of underdeveloped greater omentum

sections.heading: Patient presentation — elderly and obese
paragraphs: Elderly: Higher mortality because lax abdominal wall or obesity lead to delayed diagnosis of generalized peritonitis; atrophied omentum lead to high risk of generalized peritonitis; comorbidities
Obese: Delay in diagnosis because obesity mask all local signs of acute appendicitis

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: Essentially clinical
CBC (elevation of WBC)
Urinalysis to exclude urinary DDxs
Pregnancy test to exclude pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy in females with child bearing age
Imaging will show inflammation of appendix
US: no radiation, more available, hard to use if in patients with peritonitis
MRI: no radiation, expensive, useful for pregnant women and pediatric patients
CT scan: high radiation, more specific than US
If the findings are classic then no need for imaging

sections.heading: Alvardo score
paragraphs: Alvardo score helps you in diagnosing Acute Appendicitis
History: Migratory RIF pain — 1; Anorexia — 1; Nausea or vomiting — 1
Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness — 2; Rebound tenderness — 1; Fever — 1
Laboratory: Leukocytosis — 2; Shift to left — 1
Total — 10

sections.heading: Alvardo score interpretation
paragraphs: Score 1–4: low risk appendicitis => check your differential diagnoses
Score 5–6: equivocal, Send for imaging (US, CT scan, MRI)
7 and more: strongly predictive for acute appendicitis
For Alvardo score of 5 or higher obtain early surgical consultation before sending to imaging

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Surgical: Pre OP preparations: IV fluids; Antibiotics
Generally to cover enteric content (gram negatives and anaerobes)
Ciprofloxacin/metronidazole, 2nd or 3rd generation cephalosporin can be used instead of ciprofloxacin
Non surgical if there is no complications and not preferred in general because of recurrence
Bowel rest
IV antibiotics

sections.heading: Definition
paragraphs: Joint infection by microorganisms
Mostly affect children less than 3 years old
Bacteria are the most significant pathogen because of their rapidly destructive nature
Non gonococcal and gonococcal bacterial septic arthritis
Non gonococcal: very aggressive. Staphylococcal infection (mostly S. aureus); Group A strep (strep pyogenes)
Gonococcal: caused by Neisseria gonorrhea. Most common 75% of cases of septic arthritis

sections.heading: Presentation
paragraphs: Progressive swelling of joint
Overlying skin of joint is warm and erythematous
Single joint but sometimes more than one is involved especially in neonates and younger children
Most commonly affected joints: hip, knee, ankle, elbow, wrist, shoulder
The joint is extremely tender
Patient unwilling to move their joint, the joint is held in position of most comfort, usually slight flexion
Onset is insidious and rapid
Systemic symptoms like fever, weakness, and headache

sections.heading: Attention!
paragraphs: Don’t overlook septic arthritis in joints that already have gout or rheumatoid arthritis
Sometimes the patient can move their joint because they already took steroids and analgesics over the counter which mask the inability to move
Sometimes the signs of septic joint is masked by antibiotics
IV drug abusers may have involvement of uncommon joints of the axial skeleton (eg sacroiliac, vertebral, sternoclavicular joints)

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: If you suspect septic arthritis then:
Order FBC, ESR, CRP
Blood cultures, throat cultures
Joint aspiration is definitive but maybe delayed while waiting for laboratory studies
X ray may be initially normal or show only soft tissue swelling with displacement of capsular fat planes, later, features of bone destruction

sections.heading: Synovial fluid analysis
paragraphs: Normal / Septic arthritis
Color: Transparent / Yellow
Appearance: Clear / Purulent, turbid
Special tests/crystals: Normal string sign / Gram stain, culture

sections.heading: Kocher criteria
paragraphs: Four criteria’s
Unable to weight bear the affected side — 1 point
ESR > 40 — 1 point
Fever > 38.5 C — 1 point
WBC > 12000 — 1 point
1 point: 3%; 2 points: 40%; 3 points: 93%; 4 points: 99%

sections.heading: Types of microorganisms
paragraphs: Think gonococcal if: arthritis is migratory, monoarticular; patient is young and sexually active; slower onset of symptoms over several days; patient have symptoms of genital infection
If you don’t find purulent synovial fluid aspirate then you look for the triad (periarthritis, tenosynovitis, polyarthralgia)
Rash seen in Neisseria species in general
Think non gonococcal if: Aspiration of joint fluid reveal large number of WBCs and gram stain and cultures positive

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: IV antibiotics
Staphylococcus species: IV vancomycin or IV clindamycin
When staphylococcus infect prosthetic joint then rifampin is added to the above
N gonorrhea: IV ceftriaxone followed by oral cefixime
Refer to orthopedic team for joint irrigation/drainage especially if non gonococcal
Analgesia
Splintage of the joint

sections.heading: Definition
paragraphs: Decrease blood supply to part of the heart, causing damage to heart muscle

Mechanism: Atherosclerosis: gradual buildup of cholesterol and fibrous tissue in plaques in the walls of coronary arteries => plaques become unstable, rupture and promote formation of a blood clot that blocks the artery => MI
Prinzmetal’s angina: spasm of coronary arteries
Other causes: anemia, hyperthyroidism...
Cardiac enzymes are the gold standard for diagnosing Myocardial infarction
Anatomy: Left anterior descending artery; Left Circumflex artery; Right coronary artery

sections.heading: ACS
paragraphs: Unstable angina: worsening of already existing angina. Chest pain at rest or with previously tolerated exertion. Cardiac enzymes: negative
STEMI: transmural infarct involves the permanent occlusion of LAD artery or LCx or RCA. Cardiac enzymes: positive
NSTEMI: non transmural infarct involves the transient/partial obstruction of coronary artery, or small intramural vessel obstruction. Cardiac enzymes: positive

sections.heading: Patient presentation — classic presentation, STEMI and NSTEMI
paragraphs: Chest pain (tightness, squeezing, pressure, crushing), retrosternal, poorly localized
Anginal chest pain lasts from 2 to 10 minutes and brought on by exertion and relieved by rest
Unstable angina pain lasts from 10 to 30 minutes and it is chest pain at rest
MI pain lasts longer than 30 minutes
Chest wall tenderness
Radiation of the pain to the arms, neck, jaw
Sweating, dyspnea, nausea or vomiting

sections.heading: Patient presentation — non classic presentation, STEMI and NSTEMI
paragraphs: Occur more frequently in females, racial minorities, diabetics, elderly, patients with altered mental status
Chest pain lasting for seconds, or constant pain lasting for 12 to 24 hours without change in intensity
Dyspnea at rest or with exertion without chest pain
Shoulder, arm or jaw discomfort without chest pain
Nausea
Generalized weakness
Diaphoresis

sections.heading: Watch Out!
paragraphs: Do not exclude ACS if the ECG is normal, examination is normal or patient is < 30 years old
Epigastric or upper abdominal discomfort, even when relieved with antacids, raises suspicion for ACS, especially for patient > 50 years old or those with known CAD

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: ECG
Cardiac enzymes
Blood tests: Electrolyte: derangements predispose to arrhythmia
CBC: to identify secondary causes of NSTEMI like anemia and blood loss
Liver function tests: useful if patient take drugs that undergo hepatic metabolism
BUN and creatinine: for patients taking drugs renally excreted and to asses kidney function in patient with CKD

sections.heading: ECG (STEMI) — hyperacute changes
paragraphs: In the first few hours after the myocardial infarction
Tall, widened T waves
Upward sloping ST segment: ST segment lose normal upward concavity, then straightens and slopes upward before becoming elevated

Increase ventricular activation time: interval between the start of the QRS and the apex of the R wave more than > 0.045 sec, because the infarcting myocardium is slower to conduct electrical impulses
Increase height of R wave in inferior leads in inferior MI

sections.heading: ECG (STEMI) — acute and chronic changes
paragraphs: Acute changes: Start few hours after the MI and continue for hours or days
ST elevation: significant if elevated > 1mm in 2 limb leads, or > 2mm in 2 adjacent chest leads, this is the most important ECG change
Reciprocal ST depression may occur on the opposite leads
Pathological Q waves: reflect electrically inert necrotic myocardium
Conduction problem may develop, like LBBB, RBBB
Chronic changes: Permanent changes that start few weeks after MI; Q waves remain; Everything else goes back to normal

sections.heading: ECG (STEMI localization)
paragraphs: Location — Leads — Coronary artery
Inferior — II, III, aVF — RCA 80%, LCx 18%
Anterior — V2–V4 — LAD
Anteroseptal — V1–V4 — LAD
Lateral — I, aVL, v5, v6 — LCx
Posterior — ST depression in V1, V2; ST elevation in V7, V8 — RCA
Anterior — LBBB — LAD

sections.heading: ECG (NSTEMI)
paragraphs: It could be normal
Horizontal or down sloping ST depression > 0.5 mm
Symmetrically inverted T waves > 2 mm
Diffuse precordial ST depression more pronounced in leads V4–V6 may indicate a stenosis in the mid LAD artery and if changes evident in leads V2–V3 it is more suggestive of stenosis of the LCx artery

Diffuse ST depression including both precordial and extremity leads associated with ST elevation > or = to 1mm in lead aVR may indicate stenosis in the left main coronary artery, or proximal occlusion in the LAD

sections.heading: Cardiac enzymes
paragraphs: Gold standard in diagnosing STEMI and NSTEMI
Elevated in STEMI and NSTEMI
Troponin I: begins to elevate approximately 6 hours after the onset of chest pain and remains elevated for 1 week
CK-MB: specific for cardiac muscle, begins to elevate 6 hours after the onset of chest pain and peaks within 24 hours, normalize in 72 hours post MI

sections.heading: Treatment (STEMI)
paragraphs: PCI (percutaneous intervention) angioplasty with stenting is the treatment of choice for STEMI
If PCI cannot be performed within 90 minutes of diagnosis then thrombolytic therapy is an alternative, benefits reduce with time
Thrombolytic therapy risk exceeds benefits after 12 hours of diagnosis
Thrombolytic therapy (tPA, streptokinase)
Absolute contraindications: hemorrhagic strokes, non hemorrhagic strokes with 3 months, active internal bleeding, aortic dissection, head and facial trauma in last 3 months
Relative contraindications: Hx of severe hypertension, BP of 180/110, major surgery or trauma within month, allergy to streptokinase, active peptic ulcer disease, current use of anticoagulation

sections.heading: Treatment (STEMI, NSTEMI, unstable angina) — beta blockers
paragraphs: Beta blockers: slow heart rate
Decrease mortality associated with myocardial infarctions
Atenolol: 5 mg slowly IV over 5min, repeated once after 15 min

Metoprolol: initial dose 5 mg IV every 2 minutes as tolerated for 3 doses then if patient tolerated the first 3 doses then give 50mg orally every 6 hours starting 15 minutes after the last IV dose and if patient intolerant of full IV dose then you give 25 to 50mg according to their clinical condition
Contraindicated in uncontrolled heart failure, hypotension, bradyarrhythmias, COPD

sections.heading: Treatment — nitrates and morphine
paragraphs: Nitrates: pain relief and decrease afterload
Three doses of sublingual nitrate 0.4mg every 5 minutes if no pain relief then
IV nitroglycerin: dose should be titrated upwards until symptoms are relieved, and in hypertensive patients until blood pressure normalized
Careful blood pressure monitoring while giving nitrate
When Side effect like hypotension and headaches occur nitrates should be stopped
Nitrate contraindicated if patient took phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor within 24 hours, it cause severe hypotension
Morphine: pain relief and decrease afterload
Dose of 2–8 mg repeated at intervals of 5 to 15 minutes until pain relieved or side effects occur

sections.heading: Treatment — oxygen, aspirin and heparin
paragraphs: Oxygen: Only in patients who are hypoxemic (arterial oxygen saturation < 90%) or who have respiratory distress
Aspirin: make blood thinner
Decrease mortality associated with myocardial infarction
Give 160–325mg per oral aspirin within minutes of presentation if patient can’t take oral medications then give 300–600mg per rectum
Then continue with maintenance dose of 81–325mg everyday
IV heparin: prevent further thrombus formation
